Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: No credible evidence found of government revenue collection (tax/customs/fees) being digitized via national payment gateways in authoritative sources during this pass.

revision_notes: Original score was Unknown with no source cited. A single light Exa search surfaced substantial authoritative evidence, so the row was escalated to the full verification path. Sudan Customs has operated an electronic payment channel for clearance since at least April 2025, credited with increasing revenue collection. The Ministry of Finance signed a 'My Payment' contract with National Workers' Bank (April 2026) to enable electronic payment of government fees, and the Central Bank completed core-banking integration with the Ministry of Finance's 'Esali' payment system (June 2026). The Tax Chamber's own e-payment channel is still described by the Tax Chamber itself as being progressively activated rather than fully rolled out. Recalculated to 2 (Partial): specific revenue streams are digitally payable and operational, but comprehensive digital tax payment is not yet complete.
revised_comments: Customs duties are collected electronically nationwide, a change credited with increasing revenue and speeding clearance. Since 2026 the Ministry of Finance has rolled out a 'My Payment' electronic channel (with National Workers' Bank) for government fees, and the Central Bank of Sudan has integrated its core banking system with the Ministry of Finance's Esali payment platform for real-time government account data exchange. The Tax Chamber's own online tax-payment channel remains under phased rollout rather than fully operational across all offices and tax types, so overall digital coverage of revenue collection is partial rather than comprehensive.

revised_comments: The Sudan Tax Chamber (SudanTax) operates an official E-Portal at tax.gov.sd enabling taxpayers to register remotely, obtain a tax identification number, file and amend returns electronically, view account activity, and request clearance certificates. An electronic payment channel is being progressively activated, including a remote e-portal payment option and point-of-sale channels within tax offices, with rollout continuing across the states. The portal therefore combines a mature e-filing service with a payment function still under active development.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: Evidence of active national-scale G2P digitization was not found in authoritative sources during this pass. While the Better Than Cash Alliance release discusses intentions for the Sudan Family Support Program to deliver digital transfers to ~80% of families, it is a commitment/plan rather than evidence of implemented, ongoing nationwide G2P rails in operation, and I did not locate an implementation report with disbursement evidence.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score was Unknown, on the basis that the Sudan Family Support Programme (SFSP) commitment was only a plan without implementation evidence. Fuller research found a World Bank publication, 'Delivering Hope in Fragile Times', confirming the SFSP actually disbursed digital cash transfers via a modular automated payment platform (mobile credit, mobile wallet, bank transfer, or cash), reaching 8.7 million people (50% women) before the programme was suspended in 2021 following the political transition. Digital G2P activity today continues only via humanitarian actors such as WFP, not as a resumed government programme. Recalculated to 2 (Limited Use): large-scale digital G2P has been demonstrated historically but is not currently active as a government-run programme.
revised_comments: The Sudan Family Support Programme (2020-2021) delivered monthly digital cash transfers to eligible families using a modular, automated payment platform, giving recipients a choice of mobile credit, mobile wallet, bank transfer, or cash. It reached 8.7 million people, half of them women, before being suspended following the political transition of October 2021. Government-to-person digitisation is not currently operating at that scale; ongoing cash transfers to vulnerable populations are chiefly delivered by humanitarian agencies, such as the World Food Programme, using mixed cash, e-voucher, and mobile money/bank channels rather than as a resumed government programme.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: No credible evidence found of a dedicated consumer protection framework for digital payments (e.g., payment services consumer protection regulation, e-money consumer protection directive, or ombudsman specific to payments). Searches on CBOS site and web for “consumer protection” + payments/mobile money in Sudan did not yield a clearly applicable framework.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score was Unknown; a search for a dedicated consumer protection framework did not surface one. Fuller research found Sudan's Regulation on Electronic Fund Transfers 2013 sets out detailed consumer protections for electronic/digital payments, including error resolution, liability for unauthorised use, refund rights, and disclosure requirements, as documented in a 2015 UNCTAD paper by Sudan's Ministry of Trade. A 2023 UNCDF diagnostic confirms CBOS has a department handling consumer protection and complaints, but notes the framework is fragmented across several laws, lacks a dedicated digital-channel recourse mechanism, and that CBOS is still developing a standalone consumer protection framework. Recalculated to 2 (Partial): sectoral/general protections exist but no comprehensive dedicated framework.
revised_comments: Consumer protection for digital payments in Sudan rests mainly on the 2013 Regulation on Electronic Fund Transfers, which sets rules on authorisation of transfers, erroneous payments, liability for unauthorised use, and customer refund rights, alongside general provisions in the Civil Transactions Act 1984 and the Electronic Transactions Act 2007. The Central Bank of Sudan maintains a unit handling consumer protection and complaints and is developing a dedicated financial consumer protection framework, but current provisions are scattered across multiple laws, enforcement is inconsistent, and there is no purpose-built recourse mechanism for digital payment channels.

revision_notes: Original score was Unknown, noting the absence of a data protection act. Research confirms this via Data Protection Africa's Sudan country fact sheet, which explicitly states there is no law requiring notification to a data protection authority or to affected data subjects in the event of a data breach. A generic legal-blog source claimed a 72-hour mandatory breach-notification requirement, but this could not be corroborated against Sudanese statute and conflicts with the specialist Data Protection Africa tracker, so it is treated as unreliable. Recalculated to 1 (No): no mandatory or discretionary breach-notification regime exists.
revised_comments: Sudan has no data protection legislation and, correspondingly, no legal requirement for payment service providers or other data controllers to notify users, regulators, or a data protection authority in the event of a data breach or cybersecurity incident. The country's cybercrime statutes, including the Informatic Offences Act 2007 and the Cyber Crime Prevention Act as amended in 2020, criminalise unauthorised access to and disclosure of data but do not impose affirmative breach-notification duties on organisations.

The Electronic Banking Services Company, the CBOS's payments-processing arm, has also released periodic reports on interbank transfer volumes to the media, most recently reporting more than 141 million interbank transactions in the first half of 2026. Reporting cadence is at least annual, with some additional ad hoc disclosures.

Field research with Organisations of Persons with Disabilities indicates that economic hardship limits phone ownership among persons with disabilities, restricting their access to mobile-money applications, and that documentation barriers, including under-registration of births for children with disabilities, compound financial exclusion.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: No credible evidence found of formal refugee/migrant access mechanisms to digital payments (e.g., special KYC measures, UNHCR-linked wallet programs) with clear, current operational detail in authoritative sources during this pass.

revision_notes: Original score was Unknown citing no formal mechanism found. Research located a detailed FSD Africa/Strategic Impact Advisors report confirming that in 2019 the Central Bank of Sudan issued a decree recognising the Commission of Refugees (COR) identity card as a valid KYC document for opening financial accounts and registering SIM cards. However, acceptance is inconsistent: some banks and mobile network operators accept the COR card alone, others require an additional COR confirmation letter, and some do not recognise it at all; there is also uncertainty over whether the 2019 circular remains in force following the change in government. Recalculated to 2 (Partial): a formal legal pathway exists but practical access is inconsistent.
revised_comments: Refugees and displaced persons in Sudan have a formal, if inconsistently applied, pathway to financial access. A 2019 Central Bank of Sudan decree recognises the Commission of Refugees (COR) identity card as an acceptable KYC document for opening bank accounts and registering SIM cards. In practice, acceptance varies: some financial service providers and mobile network operators accept the COR card alone, others require an accompanying confirmation letter from the Commission of Refugees, and some do not recognise it at all, leaving many refugees reliant on SIM cards registered in others' names. Uncertainty also remains over whether the 2019 circular is still applied following subsequent changes in government.
